chapters.title: Chapter 1: Foundations of Currency Valuation Theory

lessons.title: Why We Need Theories of Currency Valuation: Fair Value vs Market Price

children.text: On any given day, USD/INR might trade at 83.20 in the morning and 83.45 by evening. Ask five economists what the rupee is actually worth and you will get five different numbers, none of which is 83.20 or 83.45. This is not a contradiction. The price on your screen and the value a theory computes are answering two different questions, and mixing them up is the single most common mistake retail and HNI investors make when reading currency news.

body.text: Market price is what a currency actually trades for right now, set by supply and demand in the forex market. Fair value, also called the equilibrium exchange rate, is what a specific economic theory, such as purchasing power parity or interest rate parity, calculates the currency should trade for. The two can differ for years at a stretch.

children.text: Market Price: What the Screen Actually Shows You

markDefs.definition: The wholesale market where banks and large financial institutions trade currencies directly with each other, in large sizes, at the rates that ultimately filter down to the RBI reference rate, NSE futures and retail forex quotes.

children.text: The number you see, whether it is the RBI's daily reference rate, the price on NSE currency futures, or the rate your bank quotes on a forex card, is a market price. It is set the same way any traded asset's price is set: by whoever is willing to buy or sell dollars for rupees at that moment in the
, adjusted instantly for news, capital flows and sentiment. A market price answers exactly one question: what will the rupee actually fetch if you trade it right now.
Fair Value: What a Theory Says the Rate Should Be

markDefs.definition: The theoretical exchange rate implied by a specific economic model, distinct from the price actually observed in the market at any given moment.

children.text: , is a different animal entirely. It is not observed in any market, it is calculated. An economist applying purchasing power parity might compute that USD/INR should be 74 based on relative price levels in India and the US. Another applying interest rate parity might compute a completely different forward-looking number based on the RBI repo rate and the Fed funds rate. Neither of these is wrong, and neither of them is what you will actually pay at a bank counter today. They are answering a different question: given a specific economic relationship, where should the rate be pulled toward over time?

children.text: Why the Two Diverge, and for How Long

Market price is dominated minute to minute by forces that have nothing to do with fair-value theory: FII and FPI flows chasing yield or fleeing risk, RBI intervention to smooth volatility, speculative positioning, and plain sentiment around a Fed or RBI policy decision. Fair value moves only when its underlying inputs move, and those inputs (inflation differentials, interest rate gaps) change slowly, over quarters and years, not minutes. That mismatch in speed is exactly why the two can sit far apart for a long time without any forced correction.

body.text: The Big Mac Index has flagged the rupee as significantly undervalued against the dollar in essentially every reading since the Economist began tracking India, using the Maharaja Mac (the chicken-based equivalent sold here, since Indian outlets do not serve beef) as the local benchmark. That persistent undervaluation has never forced the rupee to appreciate on any fixed schedule. Fair value is a gravitational pull, not a deadline.

body.caption: How economists measure the size of a currency's over- or under-valuation: S_t is today's market price, S_t* is the theory's fair value estimate. This course's remaining chapters build out two ways to calculate S_t*.

children.text: Why This Distinction Matters for You as an Investor

If you are an HNI allocating offshore, or an angel investor holding dollar-denominated stakes, the practical risk is conflating fair value with a trading signal. Investors who do this often hedge too early, hold a hedge too long waiting for a correction that has no deadline, or skip hedging altogether because a report says the rupee is cheap and due to strengthen. The RBI itself publishes a real effective exchange rate (REER) reading every month as its own fair-value-adjacent benchmark, and even that feeds into policy commentary, not a trading rulebook.

body.title: Fair Value Says Cheap, the Screen Says Otherwise
body.scenario: An HNI client reads a report stating the rupee is undervalued by roughly 30% against the dollar based on purchasing power parity. Excited, they ask their advisor to go all-in on a rupee-strengthening bet, expecting a sharp rally within the next few months.
body.prompt: What is wrong with acting on this single data point alone? What does 'undervalued by 30% on PPP' actually tell you, and what does it not tell you?
body.modelAnswer: PPP undervaluation tells you almost nothing about timing. The rupee has traded undervalued by similar or larger margins on Big Mac Index style readings for most of the last decade and more, without staging a matching rally within any predictable window. PPP is a long-run anchor best read over five to ten year horizons, not a short-term trading trigger. Before acting, the advisor should also check interest rate differentials (interest rate parity, covered later in this course), current FII and FPI flow trends, the RBI's own REER reading, and the current account position. A single fair-value estimate from one theory is one input, not a standalone buy or sell signal.

body.title: Quick Check
body.question: Which of the following best describes 'fair value' as used in currency valuation theory?
options: The exact rate a bank will quote you for a transaction today
A theoretical benchmark calculated from an economic model, distinct from the tradable market price
The average of the last 30 days of spot rates
The rate set once a year by the RBI's Monetary Policy Committee
body.explanation: Fair value is a model output, not a tradable quote. It is calculated using a specific economic relationship, such as PPP or interest rate parity, and describes where a currency should trade based on that relationship's assumptions, not what you would actually pay or receive in a transaction today.

cards.definition: The rate a currency actually trades at right now in the interbank forex market.
The rate a specific economic theory, such as PPP or interest rate parity, calculates a currency should trade at.
The RBI's own trade-weighted, inflation-adjusted index used to judge whether the rupee is over- or undervalued against a basket of currencies.
The percentage difference between a currency's market price and its theoretical fair value at a given point in time.

points: Market price is what a currency actually trades for right now; fair value is what an economic theory calculates it should trade for. They answer different questions.
Market price is set by supply, demand, capital flows and sentiment in the interbank forex market, and moves every second markets are open.
Fair value is calculated from slower-moving inputs like inflation differentials or interest rate gaps, and can stay far from market price for years without correcting.
A currency being 'undervalued' by a theory like PPP is not a trading signal on its own, it is one input among several, alongside interest rate parity, capital flows and the RBI's own REER reading.
The rest of this course builds out the two main frameworks used to estimate fair value: purchasing power parity in Chapter 2, and interest rate parity in Chapter 3.
